content: The presence of harmful mutations in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes significantly increases the risk of developing certain cancers, including breast cancer and high-grade serous cancers (HGSC) of ovarian, fallopian tube, and peritoneal origin. Risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO) is commonly recommended for women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations after they have completed childbearing. However, despite previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses, the effectiveness of RRSO in reducing cancer-related mortality and incidence remains a topic of debate, particularly regarding differences in outcomes based on the specific mutation type. The objective of this study was to evaluate the benefits and harms of RRSO in women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations. A comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, and trial registries, was conducted up to July 2017 without language restrictions. Abstracts from scientific meetings and other relevant publications were also reviewed. The study included non-randomized trials, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, and case series that used statistical adjustments for baseline differences. Comparisons were made between women who underwent RRSO and those who did not, excluding individuals with a history of breast, ovarian, or fallopian tube cancer. Data from 10 cohort studies involving 8,087 participants were analyzed. Of these, 2,936 women underwent RRSO, while 5,151 served as controls. The studies compared RRSO, with or without risk-reducing mastectomy (RRM), to no RRSO (surveillance). The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to significant risks of bias. Meta-analyses were performed using hazard ratios (HR) for time-to-event outcomes and risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled effect estimates, and inconsistency between studies was assessed using the I² statistic. The main findings were as follows: 1. Overall Survival: Women who underwent RRSO had longer overall survival compared to those who did not (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.54; P < 0.001). However, the certainty of this evidence was very low. 2. High-Grade Serous Cancer (HGSC) Mortality: RRSO was associated with a significant reduction in HGSC-related mortality (HR 0.06, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.17; P < 0.0001). The certainty of this evidence was also very low. 3. Breast Cancer Mortality: RRSO was linked to a reduction in breast cancer mortality (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.88; P = 0.009). Again, the certainty of this evidence was very low. 4. Quality of Life: One study reported improved quality of life related to ovarian cancer risk perception in women who underwent RRSO (MD 15.40, 95% CI 8.76 to 22.04; P < 0.00001). However, the evidence was of very low certainty. 5. Adverse Events: None of the included studies reported data on bone fracture incidence or severe adverse events related to RRSO. Subgroup analyses revealed the following: Among BRCA1 mutation carriers, RRSO was associated with increased overall survival (HR 0.30, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.52; P < 0.001) and reduced HGSC mortality (HR 0.10, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.41; P = 0.001). Breast cancer mortality was also lower in this group (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.67; P < 0.0001). For BRCA2 mutation carriers, RRSO was associated with increased overall survival (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.85; P = 0.01). However, the effect on HGSC mortality was uncertain due to the low frequency of HGSC-related deaths in this group. There was no significant reduction in breast cancer mortality (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.87; P = 0.75). One study suggested that RRSO combined with RRM may improve overall survival (HR 0.14, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.98; P = 0.0001), but it did not significantly reduce breast cancer mortality (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.19; P = 0.25). The timing of RRSO (before or after age 50) did not appear to influence breast cancer mortality for either BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation carriers. In conclusion, the evidence supporting the benefits of RRSO in increasing overall survival and reducing HGSC and breast cancer mortality in women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations is of very low certainty. The findings suggest that RRSO may be more beneficial for BRCA1 mutation carriers than for BRCA2 mutation carriers, particularly in reducing HGSC and breast cancer mortality. However, the results should be interpreted with caution due to the limitations of the included studies, including potential biases and low-certainty evidence. Further research is needed to clarify the effects of RRSO on quality of life, adverse events, and outcomes based on mutation type and age at surgery.
